content.title: About
content.content: The Big Mac is McDonald's signature double‑burger, made of two beef patties, special sauce, lettuce, cheese, pickles and onions, all stacked between three sesame seed buns.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Big Mac was first introduced in 1967 in Pittsburgh.
Its famous tagline “Two all‑beef patties, special sauce, lettuce, cheese, pickles, onions on a sesame seed bun” is known worldwide.
In 1975 the Big Mac Index was created by The Economist as a simple way to compare purchasing power parity across countries.
The Big Mac arrived in Russia in the early 1990s and quickly became a menu staple.
A vegetarian version called the Veggie Mac replaces the beef patties with plant‑based patties.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The two beef patties provide roughly 25 g of high‑quality protein, essential for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef supplies heme iron, which is readily absorbed and supports oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The slice of cheese adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and the bun contribute B12, B6 and niacin, which help with energy metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Lettuce and pickles contribute a modest amount of fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: A single Big Mac contains about 540 kcal, which can contribute to weight gain if eaten frequently.

items.title: Saturated fat and sodium
items.content: The sandwich is rich in saturated fats and salt, which may increase cardiovascular risk when consumed in excess.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: It contains gluten (bun), dairy (cheese) and soy (in the special sauce), which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some ingredients include additives that may not be suitable for people with sensitivities.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The Big Mac is typically served in its branded wrapper. Eat it by hand, optionally splitting it in half, and pair it with fries and a drink. For a lighter option, some replace the regular bun with a whole‑grain version.

content.title: Storage
content.content: If not eaten immediately, store the Big Mac in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, reheat in a microwave or oven to restore the bun’s texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Sourdough bread is a whole‑grain loaf made with a natural starter cultivated from wild yeasts and lactic‑acid bacteria. The dough rises slowly, giving the crust a crisp snap and a tangy aroma. Because of the long fermentation, it is often considered healthier than commercial yeast breads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sourdough starters have been used for over 5,000 years, dating back to ancient Egypt.
Extended fermentation increases B‑vitamins and minerals compared with standard breads.
Sourdough bread has a lower glycemic index, making it better for blood‑sugar control.
Traditional recipes require at least two days to develop a mature starter.
The acidity of the starter (pH 3.5‑4.0) inhibits pathogenic bacteria, extending shelf life.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Fermentation produces live lactic‑acid bacteria that support gut microbiota.

items.title: Lowers glycemic response
items.content: Slow breakdown of starch during fermentation leads to slower carbohydrate absorption.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Sourdough provides thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Heart‑healthy
items.content: Whole grains supply fiber, which helps reduce cholesterol levels.

items.title: Improves mineral absorption
items.content: Fermentation reduces phytic acid, allowing better uptake of iron and zinc.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Like any wheat bread, sourdough contains gluten and can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some recipes use a noticeable amount of salt; those monitoring sodium should check the label.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The higher acidity may irritate the stomach of individuals with gastritis or ulcer disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bread fresh, toasted, or as the base for sandwiches, soups, and salads. It pairs well with olive oil, avocado, cheese, fish, and vegetable spreads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the loaf in a paper bag or linen sack at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven before serving to restore crust crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Quail eggs are small speckled eggs of the Japanese quail (Coturnix japonica). A single egg weighs about 10 grams, several times less than a chicken egg. The taste is delicate, similar to chicken egg, with a yolk that is large relative to the egg's size. The eggs are boiled, fried, and added to salads, appetizers, and Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: One chicken egg is roughly equal in weight to four or five quail eggs.
Quail eggshells are speckled and thin, with a tough membrane underneath.
Quail eggs take only 2–4 minutes to hard-boil.
They are often served in salads, on appetizer skewers, in soups, and in Asian dishes.
Claims that quail eggs are hypoallergenic are not scientifically supported.

items.title: Source of complete protein
items.content: The egg provides protein with all the essential amino acids.

items.title: Contain vitamin B12 and riboflavin
items.content: These vitamins support metabolism and the formation of blood cells.

items.title: Contain iron
items.content: Iron is needed for oxygen transport.

items.title: Contain selenium
items.content: Selenium is a trace mineral with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contain choline
items.content: Choline is important for nervous system function and cell membranes.

items.title: Salmonella
items.content: Raw eggs, including quail eggs, may contain Salmonella; it is best not to eat them raw, especially for children, pregnant women, older adults, and people with weakened immunity.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Egg allergy is possible, including cross-reaction with chicken eggs.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol, and people with high cholesterol should discuss how many to eat with a doctor.

items.title: Small size
items.content: Whole small eggs can be a choking hazard for small children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hard-boil quail eggs for 2–4 minutes, cool them in cold water, and peel. Add them to salads, appetizers, sandwiches, soups, and rolls and Asian dishes, or fry them whole. For safety, the white and yolk should be fully set.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store eggs in the refrigerator in their original package, away from strong-smelling foods, and use them before the expiration date. Do not wash them in advance. Keep boiled eggs in the refrigerator for a few days. Discard cracked eggs and eggs with an unpleasant smell.

rice-white-with-carrots-and-dark-green-v.title: White Rice with Carrots and Dark Green Vegetables, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: A ready‑to‑eat dish of boiled white rice combined with carrots and dark green vegetables (such as broccoli or spinach), prepared without added fat. The mix of carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals makes it a balanced, nutritious meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple source of energy in many cultures worldwide.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Dark green vegetables contain chlorophyll and high amounts of vitamin K.
The lack of added fat reduces the calorie count, making it suitable for diet plans.
Traditionally, such dishes are steamed or cooked in a steamer to preserve nutrients.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: White rice provides quick‑release carbohydrates that convert to glucose, supporting energy levels.

items.title: Vision support
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots promotes eye health and improves night vision.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Dark green vegetables are high in vitamin K and calcium, essential for bone mineralization.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: No added fat helps control calorie intake and supports healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Fiber boost
items.content: Vegetables add dietary fiber, aiding regular digestion.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes in people with diabetes.

items.title: Lack of fats
items.content: Absence of fats may reduce absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K); consider adding a small amount of healthy fat to the diet.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to rice, experiencing skin or digestive reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve as a standalone meal or as a side dish with meat, fish, or legumes. It reheats well in the microwave or on the stovetop. For extra flavor, drizzle a little olive oil or add soy sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it can be stored for up to 2 months, preferably in individual portion bags.

content.title: About
content.content: A wheat bun is a soft, slightly sweet roll made from wheat flour, commonly used as the base for sandwiches. Its airy crumb holds sauces and fillings well without becoming soggy too quickly.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional wheat buns are made from simple ingredients: wheat flour, water, yeast, salt, and a touch of sugar.
In many countries buns are shaped either round or rectangular to fit packaging and sandwich assembly lines.
Buns are often lightly toasted before serving to add a crisp crust and prevent sogginess from sauces.
In the United States the “soft roll” variant is popular, containing more fat and sugar for extra tenderness.
Whole‑grain wheat buns can be made by incorporating whole‑grain flour, boosting fiber content.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Provides a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Fiber content (in whole‑grain versions)
items.content: Whole‑grain buns are rich in dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Traditional buns have minimal fat, fitting well into balanced diets.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: Neutral flavor makes the bun compatible with a wide range of fillings, encouraging varied nutrition.

items.title: Wheat/gluten allergy
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may experience adverse reactions to wheat buns.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White wheat buns can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes, which may be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some buns contain added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Commercially produced buns may include flavor enhancers and preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use wheat buns as the foundation for sandwiches, adding meat, fish, vegetables, cheese, and sauces. Lightly toast them for a crunchy crust or enjoy them cold in a classic deli sandwich. Mini buns work well for bite‑size snacks and appetizers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep buns in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a zip‑top bag – they stay fresh for 2‑3 months. Reheat in an oven or toaster before use to restore softness.
